callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body: Before proceeding, consider: What do you already believe about how goals shape learning? Do you distinguish between wanting to *understand* something and wanting to *perform well* on it? In which contexts have you pursued one over the other — and with what consequences? Articulating your prior intuitions about goal-directed behavior will create the cognitive contrast that makes the theoretical distinctions in this report most illuminating.

callouts.title: Achievement Goal (Nicholls, 1984; Dweck, 1986; Ames, 1992)
callouts.body:
An achievement goal is a cognitively represented purpose that organizes and directs achievement behavior by establishing the standard against which competence is evaluated and success is defined. Achievement goals are not goals in the generic sense of desired outcomes — they are not simple intentions to complete tasks or perform well. They specify *how* the actor construes the meaning of competent performance: what counts as doing well, what constitutes failure, and what purposes are served by engaging in the achievement activity.

**Boundary:** An achievement goal should be distinguished from achievement *values* (the importance attached to achievement domains generally), achievement *motives* (chronic psychological needs to approach success or avoid failure, as in McClelland's and Atkinson's earlier need-achievement tradition), and task *goals* (specific intended outcomes or targets). Achievement goals are specifically about the purpose-structures that govern competence-relevant self-evaluation — the frame through which performance is interpreted, not merely the target toward which performance is directed.

**Historical Development:** The achievement goal construct emerged as a theoretical synthesis of Nicholls' developmental work on conceptions of ability, Dweck's attribution-focused work on helpless and mastery-oriented response patterns, and Ames' classroom climate research. All three converged independently on the insight that goal orientation — the purpose pursued — was more predictive of motivational outcomes than ability level per se.

**Common Misconception:** Achievement goals are frequently conflated with performance *standards* (how high the target is set) or with the *content* of what is pursued. AGT is not about the *level* of aspiration but about the *criterion by which success is defined* — a mastery-oriented student might have extremely high absolute performance standards while still defining success in terms of personal growth rather than social comparison.

**See also:** [[Achievement-Goal]], [[Goal-Orientation]], [[Mastery-Goal]], [[Performance-Goal]], [[Intrinsic-Motivation]]

callouts.title: Differentiated Conception of Ability (Nicholls, 1984)
callouts.body:
In the differentiated conception of ability, a person understands ability as a stable, capacity-like entity that is distinct from the effort expended. High ability is demonstrated when one achieves the same outcome as others with *less effort* — or superior outcomes with equivalent effort. Under this conception, expending high effort to achieve moderate performance is evidence of *low* ability, since effort is now understood as compensating for limited capacity rather than as an intrinsic contributor to achievement. This is the conception that underlies ego involvement and performance goal orientation.

**Boundary:** The differentiated conception is not a belief that effort is worthless. It is specifically the belief that ability and effort are *logically separable* in the analysis of achievement — that "real ability" is what remains when effort is controlled for. This is a cognitively sophisticated conception that typically emerges by late childhood and becomes the normative adult conception in Western competitive contexts.

**See also:** [[Differentiated-Conception-of-Ability]], [[Ego-Involvement]], [[Entity-Theory-of-Intelligence]], [[Performance-Goal-Orientation]], [[Fixed-Mindset]]

callouts.title: Undifferentiated Conception of Ability (Nicholls, 1984)
callouts.body:
In the undifferentiated conception of ability, effort and ability are not clearly distinguished — trying hard *is* what it means to be capable. Achievement is defined by learning, improvement, or task mastery rather than by normative comparison, because the actor has not yet constructed the capacity/effort distinction that would make normative superiority informationally relevant. This conception is developmentally earlier (typical in young children) but remains available to adults, particularly when task involvement and intrinsic engagement are high.

**Boundary:** The undifferentiated conception should not be understood as a confused or immature state that is simply overcome by development. Nicholls and subsequent researchers (e.g., Ames, Dweck) argued that it represents a functionally adaptive orientation toward learning contexts — one that should ideally persist alongside, rather than be displaced by, the differentiated conception.

**See also:** [[Incremental-Theory-of-Intelligence]], [[Growth-Mindset]], [[Mastery-Goal-Orientation]], [[Task-Involvement]]

callouts.title: Task Involvement (Nicholls, 1984)
callouts.body:
Task involvement is a motivational state in which the person is oriented toward developing competence, mastering the task at hand, or learning as an end in itself. The standard of success is self-referential or task-referential — one succeeds by improving, by solving the problem, by understanding more deeply. In a state of task involvement, effort is experienced as straightforwardly positive: more effort means better mastery. The differentiated conception of ability is not activated; failure does not imply incapacity.

**See also:** [[Mastery-Goal-Orientation]], [[Intrinsic-Motivation]], [[Flow]], [[Autonomous-Motivation]]

callouts.title: Ego Involvement (Nicholls, 1984)
callouts.body:
Ego involvement is a motivational state in which the person is oriented toward demonstrating or protecting judgments of their own ability relative to others. The standard of success is normative — one succeeds by outperforming peers, by demonstrating superior capacity. In a state of ego involvement, effort is instrumentally valued *only if* it produces normatively superior results; if it does not, effort expenditure provides evidence of limited capacity. This state activates the differentiated conception of ability and creates self-worth vulnerability.

**See also:** [[Ego-Involvement]], [[Performance-Goal-Orientation]], [[Entity-Theory-of-Intelligence]], [[Contingent-Self-Worth]]

callouts.title: Implicit Theory of Intelligence (Dweck & Leggett, 1988)
callouts.body:
An implicit theory of intelligence is an individual's naïve belief about the fundamental nature of intellectual ability — specifically, whether it is a fixed entity of limited stock (entity theory) or a malleable quality that can be developed through effort and learning (incremental theory). These beliefs are "implicit" in the sense that they function as background assumptions that organize goal pursuit, attribution, and persistence, rather than as explicit philosophical positions the person articulates or defends.

**Boundary:** Implicit theories of intelligence are not beliefs about one's *current* level of intelligence — they are beliefs about the *nature* of intelligence as such. A person can hold an incremental theory while simultaneously believing that their current skills are limited; they differ from the entity theorist in believing that those skills can fundamentally improve, not that they are already high.

**Common Misconception:** The popular discourse on "growth mindset" (Dweck's applied articulation of incremental theory) has sometimes conflated the implicit theory construct with simple optimism, praise recipients, or belief in the power of effort. Dweck's original construct is specifically about the *ontological status* of ability — whether it is fixed by nature or susceptible to fundamental growth — not about effort per se.

**See also:** [[Implicit-Theory-of-Intelligence]], [[Incremental-Theory-of-Intelligence]], [[Entity-Theory-of-Intelligence]], [[Growth-Mindset]], [[Fixed-Mindset]]

callouts.title: The Tripartite Convergence
callouts.body: The simultaneous but independent convergence of Nicholls, Dweck, and Ames on the dichotomous mastery/performance distinction is one of the strongest validations of the core constructs. Three researchers, using different methods, working in different theoretical traditions (developmental psychology, social-cognitive learning theory, educational ecology), arrived at functionally equivalent constructs. This convergent validity substantially increases confidence that the mastery/performance distinction is tracking something real in the psychology of achievement.

callouts.title: 2×2 Achievement Goal Framework (Elliot & McGregor, 2001)
callouts.body:
The 2×2 framework organizes achievement goals along two orthogonal dimensions: (1) the *definition* dimension (mastery vs. performance — the competence standard used) and (2) the *valence* dimension (approach vs. avoidance — whether positive or negative possibilities regulate behavior). The resulting four goals are: **Mastery-Approach** (pursuing positive mastery outcomes — learning, development), **Mastery-Avoidance** (avoiding negative mastery outcomes — incompetence, failure to develop), **Performance-Approach** (pursuing positive performance outcomes — outperforming others, demonstrating superiority), and **Performance-Avoidance** (avoiding negative performance outcomes — appearing incompetent, performing worse than others).

**Boundary:** The 2×2 framework is specifically a taxonomy of achievement goals — the purposes that regulate achievement behavior. It is not a taxonomy of all goals relevant to academic contexts. Notes, tests, and grades may be desired outcomes (wanting an "A") without specifying the competence-relevant goal that governs how that outcome is pursued.

**See also:** [[Mastery-Approach-Goal]], [[Mastery-Avoidance-Goal]], [[Performance-Approach-Goal]], [[Performance-Avoidance-Goal]], [[2×2-Framework]]

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body: Consider a learning situation where you encountered significant difficulty. What happened? Did you interpret the difficulty as a signal that you were out of your depth — or as a normal part of a challenging learning process? Your interpretation almost certainly depended on the goal orientation you had adopted, consciously or not. The mechanisms explored in this phase explain *why* the same difficulty produces such radically different responses.

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body: The most robust practical implications of AGT come from classroom intervention studies — particularly the achievement goal structure manipulations conducted in middle and elementary school settings. These studies typically show that mastery-promoting classrooms produce higher intrinsic motivation, more help-seeking, and better deep learning outcomes even if standardized test performance is not always significantly different. The limitation is that most interventions are short-term; sustained goal structure shifts requiring cultural and systemic change are considerably harder to implement and evaluate.

callouts.title: The Performance-Approach Goals Controversy
callouts.body:
**The Tension:** Do performance-approach goals represent a conditionally adaptive motivational orientation (as Elliot and colleagues argue) or do they ultimately undermine the psychological foundations of genuine achievement (as the original mastery-goal proponents would maintain)?

**Position A — Conditional Adaptation (Elliot, Harackiewicz):** Performance-approach goals reliably predict higher exam grades and competitive performance achievement, particularly in contexts where normative competition is inherent. Approach motivation activates behavioral resources; the negative profiles of performance goals belong to the avoidance form. PAP goals should be part of any sophisticated motivational prescription for competitive achievement contexts.

**Position B — Long-Term Cost (Ames, Duda, Ryan & Deci):** The performance enhancement associated with PAP goals is real but narrow — it predicts grades and performance *rankings* but not deep learning, intrinsic motivation, or well-being. SDT research suggests that performance goals activate ego-involvement and controlled motivation, which produce the long-range motivational costs documented extensively in the autonomy-support literature. The "adaptive" performance enhancement may be bought at the cost of the intrinsic motivation that sustains learning over a career.

**Current Evidence:** Meta-analyses (e.g., Huang, 2012) confirm PAP goals' positive associations with achievement but negative associations with intrinsic motivation and deep processing. The cost-benefit calculation appears context-dependent: in short-term competitive evaluation contexts, PAP goals may be net-beneficial; in long-term learning contexts requiring sustained intrinsic engagement, they appear net-harmful.

**This Report's Position:** The evidence supports a context-calibrated view: PAP goals are conditionally adaptive for competitive performance tasks but structurally incompatible with the motivational conditions that optimize learning, creative problem solving, and psychological well-being. Educational systems should resist the pragmatic temptation to leverage PAP goals for performance gains at the expense of the motivational foundations of lifelong learning.

**See also:** [[Performance-Approach-Goal]], [[Intrinsic-Motivation]], [[Self-Determination-Theory-—-Foundational-Report]], [[Mastery-Goal-Orientation]]

callouts.title: Integration and Forward Momentum
callouts.body:
1. What is the single most important insight you've gained from this report? The most generative candidate is the ecological embeddedness of goal orientation: goal adoption is not fate, but it is not purely internal either — it is systematically constructed by the achievement environments we design and inhabit.
2. If you were to explain the essence of AGT to a colleague in three sentences, what would you say? Achievement Goal Theory explains why two equally capable students can thrive or fail in the same classroom: it depends on what "success" means to them. If success means development and mastery, difficulty is informative and effort is dignified. If success means outperforming peers, difficulty is threatening and effort is a confession of limited ability.
3. What is the next question worth pursuing? The most productive frontier is the integration of AGT's goal-structure account with SDT's basic needs account and CLT's cognitive architecture account in a unified theory of learning environment design — an architecture that specifies how autonomy support, mastery goal structures, and optimal cognitive load interact to produce the conditions for deep, intrinsically sustained learning.

callouts.title: Achievement Goal (Nicholls, Dweck, Ames)
callouts.body:
A cognitively represented purpose that organizes achievement behavior by specifying the standard against which competence is evaluated and success is defined. Achievement goals are not outcome targets but competence-evaluation frameworks — they specify *how* the actor construes doing well.

**Boundary:** Distinct from achievement values (domain importance), achievement motives (need-achievement), and task goals (specific intended outcomes).

**See also:** [[Achievement-Goal]], [[Goal-Orientation]], [[Achievement-Goal-Theory]], [[Mastery-Goal]], [[Performance-Goal]]

callouts.title: Mastery Goal / Mastery-Approach Goal (Ames, 1992; Elliot & McGregor, 2001)
callouts.body:
An achievement goal in which success is defined by self-improvement, task mastery, or competence development relative to prior performance or absolute task standards. In the 2×2 framework, the approach form specifically represents orientation toward positive mastery outcomes.

**Common Misconception:** Mastery goals do not preclude high absolute performance standards; they merely specify that success is self-referential or task-referenced rather than normatively comparative.

**See also:** [[Mastery-Goal-Orientation]], [[Mastery-Approach-Goal]], [[Intrinsic-Motivation]], [[Task-Involvement]], [[Mastery-Oriented-Response-Pattern]]

callouts.title: Performance Goal / Performance-Approach Goal (Ames, 1992; Elliot & Church, 1997)
callouts.body:
An achievement goal in which success is defined by normative superiority — demonstrating greater ability than others or avoiding demonstrations of inferior ability. In the 2×2 framework, the approach form seeks positive normative outcomes (outperforming); the avoidance form seeks to avoid negative normative outcomes (appearing incompetent).

**See also:** [[Performance-Goal-Orientation]], [[Performance-Approach-Goal]], [[Performance-Avoidance-Goal]], [[Ego-Involvement]], [[Differentiated-Conception-of-Ability]]

callouts.title: 2×2 Achievement Goal Framework (Elliot & McGregor, 2001)
callouts.body:
The dominant contemporary taxonomy in AGT, organizing achievement goals along two dimensions: definition (mastery vs. performance) × valence (approach vs. avoidance), generating four cells: mastery-approach, mastery-avoidance, performance-approach, performance-avoidance.

**See also:** [[2×2-Framework]], [[Mastery-Approach-Goal]], [[Mastery-Avoidance-Goal]], [[Performance-Approach-Goal]], [[Performance-Avoidance-Goal]]

callouts.title: Differentiated Conception of Ability (Nicholls, 1984)
callouts.body:
The cognitive schema in which ability is understood as a stable capacity distinct from effort — such that high ability is evidenced by achieving superior outcomes with less effort. This conception is the foundation of performance goal activation and the mechanism by which effort expenditure under failure becomes self-threatening.

**See also:** [[Differentiated-Conception-of-Ability]], [[Entity-Theory-of-Intelligence]], [[Fixed-Mindset]], [[Ego-Involvement]]

callouts.title: Ego Involvement (Nicholls, 1984)
callouts.body:
A motivational state in which the actor is oriented toward demonstrating or protecting judgments of their own ability relative to others, activating the differentiated conception of ability and making competence evaluation an ego-relevant threat rather than a learning resource.

**See also:** [[Ego-Involvement]], [[Performance-Goal-Orientation]], [[Contingent-Self-Worth]], [[Differentiated-Conception-of-Ability]]

callouts.title: Task Involvement (Nicholls, 1984)
callouts.body:
A motivational state in which the actor is oriented toward developing competence, mastering the task, or learning as an end in itself; the standard of success is self-referential or task-referential, and effort is unconditionally valuable.

**See also:** [[Mastery-Goal-Orientation]], [[Intrinsic-Motivation]], [[Flow]], [[Autonomous-Motivation]]

callouts.title: Implicit Theory of Intelligence (Dweck & Leggett, 1988)
callouts.body:
An individual's intuitive belief about whether intelligence is a fixed entity of limited stock (entity theory) or a malleable quality that grows through effort and learning (incremental theory). Entity theories predict performance goal adoption; incremental theories predict mastery goal adoption.

**See also:** [[Implicit-Theory-of-Intelligence]], [[Entity-Theory-of-Intelligence]], [[Incremental-Theory-of-Intelligence]], [[Growth-Mindset]], [[Fixed-Mindset]]

callouts.title: Helpless Response Pattern (Dweck, 1975; Dweck & Gillard, 1975)
callouts.body:
A motivational response pattern triggered by achievement difficulty or failure in performance-goal conditions, characterized by effort withdrawal, maladaptive attributions to stable factors (low ability), deteriorating performance, and negative affect — the opposite of the mastery-oriented response of maintained effort and adaptive strategy change.

**See also:** [[Helpless-Response-Pattern]], [[Learned-Helplessness]], [[Attribution-Theory]], [[Performance-Goal-Orientation]]

callouts.title: Goal Structure (Ames, 1992)
callouts.body:
The achievement goal framework embedded in a learning or organizational environment — the pattern of practices, evaluation criteria, recognition systems, and competitive norms that collectively define what "success" means within that environment and thereby shape which goals participants adopt.

**See also:** [[Mastery-Goal-Orientation]], [[Performance-Goal-Orientation]], [[Autonomy-Supportive-Environment]], [[Instructional-Design]]

callouts.title: Performance-Avoidance Goal (Elliot & Church, 1997)
callouts.body:
An achievement goal in which behavior is oriented toward avoiding demonstrations of incompetence or normative inferiority; the motivational system is organized by threat avoidance rather than positive achievement pursuit. Associated with the most adverse profile in the 2×2 taxonomy: elevated anxiety, reduced processing depth, avoidance of challenge, and poor outcomes.

**See also:** [[Performance-Avoidance-Goal]], [[Ego-Involvement]], [[Contingent-Self-Worth]], [[Helpless-Response-Pattern]], [[Attribution-Retraining]]

callouts.title: Multiple Goal Adoption
callouts.body:
The contemporaneous pursuit of more than one achievement goal within the same achievement context — most commonly mastery-approach combined with performance-approach. Research suggests this combination can be conditionally adaptive in competitive contexts, demonstrating that goals are not mutually exclusive and that goal dynamics are more complex than the dichotomous model implied.

**See also:** [[Mastery-Approach-Goal]], [[Performance-Approach-Goal]], [[Goal-Orientation]], [[Achievement-Goal-Theory]]

callouts.title: John G. Nicholls (1940–1994)
callouts.body:
Developmental and educational psychologist, University of Illinois. Nicholls' foundational contribution was the developmental analysis of ability conceptions — demonstrating that children acquire the differentiated conception of ability (distinguishing ability from effort) across middle childhood, creating the cognitive infrastructure for ego involvement. His construct of task versus ego involvement anchors one pole of the theory's history.

**Lineage:** Influenced by Atkinson's achievement motivation tradition; developed in parallel with and subsequently integrated with Dweck and Ames.

**Relationship to Report:** Provides the developmental and philosophical foundations — particularly the differentiated/undifferentiated ability distinction and the task/ego involvement construct.

callouts.title: Carol S. Dweck (1946–present)
callouts.body:
Social and developmental psychologist, Stanford University. Dweck's research program traced motivational response patterns (helpless vs. mastery-oriented) to achievement goals and subsequently to implicit theories of intelligence. Her construct of entity vs. incremental theories provides the cognitive-belief substrate that explains differential goal adoption. Her popular synthesis in *Mindset* (2006) brought the framework to wider audiences.

**Lineage:** Influenced by Seligman's learned helplessness research; collaborated with [[Ellen-Leggett]] on the 1988 paper establishing the implicit theories – goal orientation link.

**Relationship to Report:** Provides the attributional mechanism linking goal orientation to response patterns, and the implicit theories framework explaining goal adoption.

callouts.title: Carole Ames (1945–2012)
callouts.body:
Educational psychologist, Michigan State University. Ames' 1992 synthesis in *Journal of Educational Psychology* established the mastery/performance terminology that became standard and provided the most comprehensive account of how classroom goal structures shape student goal adoption. Her TARGET framework remains the cornerstone of AGT-based instructional design.

**Lineage:** Emerged from classroom motivation research; closely read Nicholls and developed the ecological dimension that was underdeveloped in his and Dweck's individual-focused work.

**Relationship to Report:** Provides the environmental/ecological account — how goal structures are instantiated by classroom practices and can be redesigned.

callouts.title: Andrew J. Elliot (1965–present)
callouts.body:
Motivational psychologist, University of Rochester. Elliot's principal contribution was the approach/avoidance extension — the insight that the mastery/performance dimension needed to be crossed with the approach/avoidance dimension to adequately account for the mixed empirical profile of performance goals. His 2×2 framework (1997, 2001) became the dominant working model.

**Lineage:** Influenced by both the AGT tradition and Atkinson's earlier approach/avoidance distinction in need-achievement theory; collaborated with McGregor, Harackiewicz, and Church on the key empirical papers.

**Relationship to Report:** Provides the contemporary 2×2 architecture that resolves the dichotomous model's inconsistencies.

callouts.title: Martin Covington (1938–present)
callouts.body:
Educational psychologist, University of California Berkeley. Covington's self-worth theory provides a critical complementary account of the performance goal system: students in performance-oriented contexts increasingly organize behavior around self-worth protection — preserving judgments of their own ability through strategic effort management, self-handicapping, and avoidance.

**Relationship to Report:** Provides the self-worth theory perspective that enriches understanding of why performance-avoidance goals develop and why they are so persistent under threatening evaluative conditions.

callouts.title: Ellen Leggett
callouts.body:
Research collaborator with Carol Dweck at Harvard and Columbia; co-authored the seminal 1988 paper establishing the implicit theories – achievement goal linkage.

**Relationship to Report:** The Dweck & Leggett (1988) paper is the foundational theoretical statement connecting implicit theories of intelligence to achievement goal adoption.

callouts.title: Dispositional Stability vs. Situational Malleability of Goal Orientation
callouts.body:
**The Tension:** To what extent is goal orientation a stable individual difference trait versus a situationally plastic state responsive to environmental framing?

**Position A — Dispositional Stability:** Measures of goal orientation show test-retest reliability comparable to personality traits; meta-analyses find individual differences in goal orientation predict outcomes over and above situational manipulations. Goal orientation may be downstream of stable entities like implicit theories of intelligence, fear of failure, or basic autonomy need satisfaction.

**Position B — Situational Plasticity:** Laboratory manipulations can reliably shift goal states using instructional framing; classroom intervention studies show sustained shifts under systematic environmental redesign. If goal orientation were purely dispositional, such shifts would be impossible.

**Current Evidence:** Both are true at different timescales. Situational factors can reliably shift goal *states* in the short term; dispositional factors determine the baseline from which situational activation occurs and the speed of recovery. The implication for intervention is that both individual-level (implicit theory change) and environmental-level (classroom goal structure redesign) targets are valid and complementary.

**This Report's Position:** A multi-level ecological view is most defensible: goal orientation reflects both dispositional tendencies and situationally activated states, with the ecological (environmental) level having the most leverage for systemic change.

**See also:** [[Goal-Orientation]], [[Implicit-Theory-of-Intelligence]], [[Autonomy-Supportive-Environment]], [[Self-Regulated-Learning]]

callouts.title: Are Goal Orientations Causes or Consequences of Achievement?
callouts.body:
**The Question:** Does mastery goal orientation *cause* better learning, or do initially successful learning experiences *produce* mastery goal orientations (because success confirms incremental theories)?

**What We Know:** The correlational literature is consistent in associating mastery goals with better outcomes. Some experimental and intervention studies show causal effects of goal orientation manipulations on cognitive engagement and outcomes.

**What We Don't Know:** The reciprocal causation question — whether achievement history shapes goal orientation at least as much as goal orientation shapes achievement — is not definitively resolved. Longitudinal studies with adequate causal modeling are relatively rare.

**Why It Matters:** If the causal arrow runs substantially from outcomes to goals (rather than vice versa), then interventions targeting goal orientation through explicit instructions or framing may be less efficacious than interventions ensuring early success experiences that biologically confirm incremental theories.

**See also:** [[Achievement-Goal-Theory]], [[Implicit-Theory-of-Intelligence]], [[Self-Efficacy]], [[Attribution-Retraining]]

callouts.title: Universality vs. Cultural Specificity of the Mastery Goal Prescription
callouts.body:
**The Tension:** Is the prescription to promote mastery goals and reduce performance goals universally valid across cultural contexts?

**Position A — Universality:** The mechanisms are cognitively fundamental (they involve how effort and ability are construed in the context of evaluative threat), so the prescriptions should be broadly applicable regardless of cultural context.

**Position B — Cultural Specificity:** In collectivist, Confucian-heritage cultures, social comparison and normative performance frames may not carry the self-worth threatening implications they carry in individualist Western contexts. The same performance goal framing that activates ego-threatening processing in an American classroom may activate cooperative, face-protecting, or family-honor-promoting goals in an East Asian classroom.

**Current Evidence:** Mixed. The basic goal constructs replicate across cultures in their structure; the *relationship* between goal orientation and outcomes shows cultural moderation, with performance goals showing less consistently adverse effects in East Asian samples.

**See also:** [[Achievement-Goal-Theory]], [[Cross-Cultural-Psychology]], [[Autonomy-Supportive-Environment]]

callouts.title: Primary Sources
callouts.body:
Nicholls, J. G. (1984). Achievement motivation: Conceptions of ability, subjective experience, task choice, and performance. *Psychological Review, 91*(3), 328–346.
*Nicholls' seminal theoretical paper establishing the differentiated/undifferentiated ability distinction and the task/ego involvement framework. The foundational theoretical document of AGT.*

Dweck, C. S., & Leggett, E. L. (1988). A social-cognitive approach to motivation and personality. *Psychological Review, 95*(2), 256–273.
*The integrative paper establishing the implicit theories – goal orientation – behavior pattern chain. Second foundational document of AGT.*

Ames, C. (1992). Classrooms: Goals, structures, and student motivation. *Journal of Educational Psychology, 84*(3), 261–271.
*Most influential single paper in AGT. Establishes mastery/performance terminology, synthesizes the field, and provides the TARGET framework for environmental design.*

Elliot, A. J., & Church, M. A. (1997). A hierarchical model of approach and avoidance achievement motivation. *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 72*(1), 218–232.
*First major statement of the 2×2 extension, introducing the performance-approach/avoidance distinction.*

Elliot, A. J., & McGregor, H. A. (2001). A 2×2 achievement goal framework. *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 80*(3), 501–519.
*The canonical statement of the 2×2 framework, extending the approach/avoidance distinction to mastery goals and providing the full four-cell taxonomy.*

callouts.title: Key Empirical Studies and Reviews
callouts.body:
Dweck, C. S. (1986). Motivational processes affecting learning. *American Psychologist, 41*(10), 1040–1048.
*Early synthesis of Dweck's research program connecting goals to response patterns.*

Ames, C., & Archer, J. (1988). Achievement goals in the classroom: Students' learning strategies and motivation processes. *Journal of Educational Psychology, 80*(3), 260–267.
*Classic empirical study demonstrating the classroom behavioral correlates of mastery vs. performance goal adoption.*

Harackiewicz, J. M., Barron, K. E., Pintrich, P. R., Elliot, A. J., & Thrash, T. M. (2002). Revision of achievement goal theory: Necessary and illuminating. *Journal of Educational Psychology, 94*(3), 638–645.
*Key paper in the debate over the rehabilitation of performance-approach goals.*

Midgley, C., et al. (2000). *Manual for the Patterns of Adaptive Learning Scales*. University of Michigan.
*Standard instrument for measuring perceived classroom goal structures and individual goal adoption; extensively used in educational intervention research.*

Huang, C. (2012). Discriminant and criterion-related validity of achievement goals in predicting academic achievement: A meta-analysis. *Journal of Educational Psychology, 104*(1), 48–73.
*Comprehensive meta-analysis confirming the differential predictive validity of the 2×2 goal cells.*

Elliot, A. J., Murayama, K., & Pekrun, R. (2011). A 3×2 achievement goal model. *Journal of Educational Psychology, 103*(3), 632–648.
*Extension to the 3×2 framework distinguishing task, self, and other referencing.*

Linnenbrink-Garcia, L., Tyson, D. F., & Patall, E. A. (2008). When are achievement goal orientations beneficial for academic achievement? Timing, individual differences, and achievement-goal contextual interactions. *International Review of Social Psychology, 21*(1–2), 19–70.
*Sophisticated analysis of moderators and context-dependence in achievement-goal-outcome associations.*

callouts.title: Reviews of Educational and Practical Applications
callouts.body:
Anderman, E. M., & Wolters, C. A. (2006). Goals, values, and affect: Influences on student motivation. In P. Alexander & P. Winne (Eds.), *Handbook of Educational Psychology* (2nd ed., pp. 369–389). Erlbaum.

Covington, M. V. (2000). Goal theory, motivation, and school achievement: An integrative review. *Annual Review of Psychology, 51*, 171–200.
*Covington's integration of self-worth theory with AGT — one of the more theoretically rich review papers.*

Kaplan, A., & Maehr, M. L. (2007). The contributions and prospects of goal orientation theory. *Educational Psychology Review, 19*(2), 141–184.
*Comprehensive review identifying unresolved theoretical issues and future directions.*

Senko, C., Hulleman, C. S., & Harackiewicz, J. M. (2011). Achievement goal theory at the crossroads: Old controversies, current challenges, and new directions. *Educational Psychologist, 46*(1), 26–47.
*Essential contemporary synthesis addressing the ongoing debates in the field.*

wiki_links.section: Phase I: Orientation & Context Setting
wiki_links.context_line: Within the landscape of educational psychology, few frameworks have generated as much empirical investigation — or as much pedagogical consequence — as [[Achievement-Goal-Theory]]. Since its emergence in the early 1980s through the convergent work of [[John-G.-Nicholls]], [[Carol-S.-Dweck]], and [[Carole-Ames]], Achievement Goal Theory (AGT) has provided a principled account of why learners who appear equally capable often diverge dramatically in their cognitive engagement, persistence, emotional responses to failure, and long-term academic development. The theory's central insight is deceptively simple but analytically powerful: the *purpose* a person pursues within an achievement context — the standard against which they define success, the criterion by which they evaluate their own competence — is not merely a psychological epiphenomenon but a *constitutive determinant* of how learning and performance unfold.

wiki_links.context_line: These two conceptions of ability anchor the two poles of the original dichotomous model of achievement goals, and they carry far-reaching implications. Under a differentiated conception, high effort is double-edged: it produces results, but if those results are not normatively superior, they simultaneously signal limited capacity. This creates the structural basis for what Dweck called the [[Helpless-Response-Pattern]] — a withdrawal of effort precisely in the contexts where persistence would be most adaptive.

Mastery Goals and Performance Goals
wiki_links.context_line: The task involvement/ego involvement distinction maps onto the dichotomous goal model's central contrast: [[Mastery-Goal-Orientation]] versus [[Performance-Goal-Orientation]]. These terms were established by Ames (1992) and are now the most widely used terminology, having largely displaced the earlier "learning goals/performance goals" (Dweck) and "task goals/ego goals" (Nicholls) nomenclature.

The Original Dichotomous Framework (1984–1996)
wiki_links.context_line: **Nicholls' Developmental Approach**. [[John-G.-Nicholls]] arrived at the goal construct through developmental psychology. His central observation was that young children and older children/adults respond to achievement failure very differently — younger children tend to persist and regulate effort upwards; older children and adults often disengage, withdraw effort, or show performance decrements after failure. The key developmental shift was the acquisition of the *differentiated conception of ability* — the capacity to understand ability as logically separate from effort. Once this conception was available, ego-involving situations activated a different processing mode: effort now threatened self-worth rather than simply being the path to mastery. Nicholls operationalized goal states as task versus ego involvement and demonstrated their systematic connections to cognition, affect, and behavior.

wiki_links.section: The Original Dichotomous Framework (1984–1996)
wiki_links.context_line: **Dweck's Attribution and Response-Pattern Approach**. [[Carol-S.-Dweck]] approached the same territory from the direction of learned helplessness and attribution theory. Her research identified two systematically different response patterns to failure: the "mastery-oriented" pattern (maintained or increased persistence, adaptive strategy changes, optimistic affect) and the "helpless" pattern (withdrawal, decreased performance, negative affect, maladaptive attributions to stable factors). The crucial theoretical move was to trace these response patterns *upstream* to the goals pursued: learners pursuing performance goals (seeking to demonstrate ability) showed [[Helpless-Response-Pattern|helpless responses]] to difficulty because failure threatened their self-judgment of ability, whereas learners pursuing learning goals (seeking to develop competence) showed mastery-oriented responses because failure was merely informative, not threatening. This insight — that goal orientation, not ability, predicts response to difficulty — was radical and has been replicated extensively. The subsequent linkage to implicit theories of intelligence enriched the framework by explaining what predicts goal adoption.

wiki_links.section: The Original Dichotomous Framework (1984–1996)
wiki_links.context_line: **Dweck's Attribution and Response-Pattern Approach**. [[Carol-S.-Dweck]] approached the same territory from the direction of learned helplessness and attribution theory. Her research identified two systematically different response patterns to failure: the "mastery-oriented" pattern (maintained or increased persistence, adaptive strategy changes, optimistic affect) and the "helpless" pattern (withdrawal, decreased performance, negative affect, maladaptive attributions to stable factors). This insight — that goal orientation, not ability, predicts response to difficulty — was radical and has been replicated extensively. wiki_links.section: The Original Dichotomous Framework (1984–1996)
wiki_links.context_line: **Ames' Classroom Climate Research**. [[Carole-Ames]] approached AGT from educational practice and classroom ecology. Her research examined how different classroom goal structures — the evaluative climate, the nature of rewards, and the student comparison norms — create different achievement goal environments that, in turn, influence which goals students adopt. Her 1992 synthesis in *Journal of Educational Psychology* is the most influential single paper in the field and introduced the now-standard mastery/performance terminology. Ames also developed the TARGET framework (Task, Authority, Recognition, Grouping, Evaluation, Time) as a structured account of how classroom practices instantiate goal structures — a critically important bridge between theory and instructional design.

wiki_links.section: The 2×2 Extension: Approach and Avoidance (1997–2011)
wiki_links.context_line: The conceptual resolution was provided by [[Andrew-Elliot]] and his collaborators. Drawing on the motivation literature's longstanding distinction between approach and avoidance motivation (rooted in Atkinson's expectancy-value model and ultimately in the basic neuroscience of behavioral activation and inhibition systems), Elliot and Church (1997) proposed the critical extension: the mastery/performance distinction should be *crossed* with the approach/avoidance distinction, generating a 2×2 matrix of achievement goals.

Mastery-Approach Goals
wiki_links.context_line: [[Mastery-Approach-Goal|Mastery-approach goals]] (MAP) represent the orientation closest to the "mastery goals" of the original dichotomous model. The person seeks to develop competence, understand the material deeply, and improve relative to their previous performance or relative to task mastery criteria. The evidence for the adaptive profile of MAP goals is robust: meta-analyses consistently link them to intrinsic motivation, cognitive engagement, persistence, positive affect, and deep processing. They are the gold standard toward which most educational interventions aim.

wiki_links.section: Performance-Approach Goals
wiki_links.context_line: [[Performance-Approach-Goal|Performance-approach goals]] (PAP) are the conceptually controversial cell in the 2×2 framework. The person seeks to outperform others, demonstrate superiority, or achieve normative excellence. Within the dichotomous framework, all performance goals were considered maladaptive. The 2×2 framework's key theoretical move was to recognize that pursuing outperformance *approaches* positive normative outcomes rather than avoiding negative ones — and that approach motivation, when successfully activated, has genuine performance benefits.

wiki_links.section: Performance-Avoidance Goals
wiki_links.context_line: [[Performance-Avoidance-Goal|Performance-avoidance goals]] (PAV) represent the most clearly adverse profile in the 2×2 taxonomy. The person seeks to avoid appearing incompetent, to not perform worse than others, or to escape negative evaluative judgments. The motivational system is organized by threat rather than by possibility. The empirical literature is consistent: PAV goals predict reduced intrinsic motivation, increased test anxiety, reduced deep processing, avoidance of challenge, and poor academic outcomes. Elliot and colleagues attribute the adverse profile to the combination of normative framing (competence defined against others) and avoidance orientation (behavior regulated by negative possibility) — a combination that maximally activates threat-based processing and self-protective cognition.

wiki_links.section: Mastery-Avoidance Goals
wiki_links.context_line: [[Mastery-Avoidance-Goal|Mastery-avoidance goals]] (MAV) were the most theoretically novel contribution of the 2×2 framework — and the most empirically contested. The person seeks to avoid failing to develop, to not reach a lower level of mastery than previously attained, or to not fall below absolute standards for task performance. Elliot and McGregor (2001) proposed this as the conceptually necessary fourth cell, and provided evidence for its existence as a distinct regulatory mode. However, MAV goals have a very different population distribution than the other three cells — they appear most prominently among perfectionists, highly conscientious individuals, experts motivated by fear of losing their skill edge, and older adults concerned about cognitive decline.

wiki_links.section: Theoretical Integration With Adjacent Frameworks
wiki_links.context_line: The relationship with SDT is particularly generative. Both frameworks analyze motivation qualitatively — both are concerned not merely with *how much* motivation but with *what kind*. Mastery goals show strong theoretical and empirical overlap with SDT's [[Intrinsic-Motivation|intrinsic motivation]] and [[Identified-Regulation|identified regulation]], while performance-avoidance goals show strong overlap with [[Introjected-Regulation|introjected regulation]] (behavior driven by internal compulsion to maintain self-worth). The frameworks differ in their primary organizing principle: AGT organizes around the *standard for competence evaluation*, while SDT organizes around the *locus of causality and psychological need satisfaction*. A comprehensive motivational account of achievement behavior benefits from both frameworks' perspectives.

wiki_links.section: Mechanism 1: Competence Attribution and Effort Interpretation
wiki_links.context_line: Under a performance goal orientation employing the differentiated conception of ability, the same effort-failure combination carries a very different implication. Because ability is construed as capacity that should be distinct from effort, high effort paired with sub-normative performance is diagnostic of low capacity. This creates the structural mechanism for the [[Helpless-Response-Pattern]]: once performance difficulties are interpreted as ability-relevant evidence, the adaptive response is to *reduce* effort (so that continued failure can be attributed to insufficient effort rather than to limited ability). This is not a failure of rationality — it is a rational response to a fundamentally misaligned goal structure.

wiki_links.section: Mechanism 2: Cognitive Engagement and Processing Depth
wiki_links.context_line: The second mechanism operates at the level of cognitive strategy selection. [[Mastery-Goal-Orientation|Mastery goals]] activate what might be called *exploratory processing* — because the purpose is understanding and genuine competence development, cognitive engagement with challenging material is intrinsically aligned with the goal. Learners pursuing mastery goals are, by construction, well-served by attending to the material's complexity, seeking connections, questioning their understanding, and investing cognitive resources in difficult passages.

wiki_links.section: Mechanism 2: Cognitive Engagement and Processing Depth
wiki_links.context_line: [[Performance-Goal-Orientation|Performance goals]], by contrast, activate *strategic-shallow processing* — because the purpose is normative demonstration, cognitive engagement is instrumentally valuable insofar as it produces demonstrable performance outputs, but exploratory depth is not reliably rewarded by the evaluation systems that matter for performance goal satisfaction. This activates what might be called *efficiency-under-evaluation* cognition: the actor seeks to produce the *outputs* (correct answers, impressive performances, normative superiority) with the minimum processing depth required, rather than investing in the comprehensive understanding that mastery goal pursuit motivates.

wiki_links.section: Mechanism 2: Cognitive Engagement and Processing Depth
wiki_links.context_line: The evidence from the cognitive engagement literature is clear on this mechanism: mastery goal adoption predicts [[Elaborative-Rehearsal|elaborative processing]], self-testing, use of help-seeking, and preferences for challenging tasks; performance goal adoption predicts surface processing, rote rehearsal, grade-strategic help-seeking, and preferences for tasks that offer high chances of demonstrating ability with low risk of demonstrating inability.

wiki_links.section: Mechanism 3: Threat Appraisal and Emotional Processing
wiki_links.context_line: The research connecting performance-avoidance goals to test anxiety is among the most robust associations in AGT's empirical record. The mechanism is clear: when one's purpose in an evaluative situation is to avoid demonstrating incompetence, every evaluative cue becomes threat-relevant. This imposes processing demands on [[Working-Memory|Working Memory]] that compete with task-relevant processing — reducing cognitive resources available for the actual task. The paradox of performance-avoidance orientation is thus mechanistically explicable: the desperate attempt to avoid failure produces the very cognitive conditions that make failure more likely.

wiki_links.section: Educational Applications
wiki_links.context_line: **Feedback design**. The implications for [[Feedback-Design-for-Autonomy-and-Mastery|feedback design]] are among the most immediately actionable. Feedback that emphasizes process and effort-in-service-of-learning (rather than ability attributions) promotes mastery orientation. Critically, praise for intelligence — a pervasive educational practice — actually undermines mastery orientation by activating the differentiated conception of ability: if intelligence is being praised, then intelligence is what is relevant, and future performances must be calibrated to protect that judgment. This counterintuitive finding (Dweck & colleagues) has been influential in changing feedback practices in educational contexts.

The Motivational Signature Matrix
wiki_links.context_line: The mastery-approach orientation's signature is characterized by: task absorption and intrinsic interest; high cognitive engagement and deep processing strategy use; persistence after failure, mediated by effort attribution rather than ability attribution; [[Formative-Feedback|formative use of feedback]] as information about learning progress rather than as evaluation of capacity; positive academic emotions (interest, enjoyment, satisfaction); and prosocial help-seeking and collaborative openness. This signature represents what Nicholls called task involvement in its most sustained, developmentally productive form.

inline_fields.value: Achievement goals — the purpose-structures that organize and direct achievement behavior — are the primary determinants of the cognitive, affective, and behavioral patterns that emerge in achievement contexts; specifically, whether a person defines success in terms of self-improvement and task mastery versus normative performance and ability demonstration produces systematically different motivational signatures that persist across time and context.

A mastery goal is an achievement goal in which success is defined by self-improvement, task mastery, and the development of competence relative to prior performance or an absolute task standard; the fundamental purpose is to develop ability rather than to demonstrate it.

A performance goal is an achievement goal in which success is defined by normative superiority — by demonstrating greater ability than others or by avoiding demonstrations of inferior ability; the fundamental purpose is to establish a favorable judgment of one's competence in the eyes of relevant evaluators.

Mastery-approach goal adoption is consistently associated with: intrinsic task motivation, information-seeking behavior (seeking additional explanations, asking questions), adaptive help-seeking, deep processing strategies, positive academic emotions (interest, enjoyment), persistence after failure, reduced test anxiety, and the development of transferable understanding rather than surface performance.

Performance-avoidance goals establish a motivational architecture in which the actor is chronically oriented toward *not failing* rather than toward *succeeding* — a regulatory mode that systematically underinvests in learning, distorts information processing toward threat evaluation, and produces what Covington termed the "self-worth protection" strategy cluster: self-handicapping, procrastination, low persistence, and strategic disengagement.

The mechanism by which performance goals produce the helpless response pattern: (1) Failure encountered → (2) Interpreted against differentiated conception of ability → (3) High effort + failure = evidence of low capacity → (4) Effort withdrawal as self-protective response to protect ability attribution → (5) Performance decrements and disengagement.

Performance-avoidance goal adoption → Competence evaluation construed as threat → Activation of threat appraisal processing (increased self-monitoring, intrusive cognition, anxiety) → Working memory competed for by threat-processing content → Reduced cognitive resources for task performance → Objective performance decrements.

Classroom practices that structure recognition around normative comparison, organize groups by ability, and evaluate on the basis of social ranking collectively instantiate a performance goal structure that, over time, shifts students' adopted goal orientations toward performance goals — even for students who entered the environment with strongly mastery-oriented dispositions.

definitions.definition: Achievement goals — the purpose-structures that organize and direct achievement behavior — are the primary determinants of the cognitive, affective, and behavioral patterns that emerge in achievement contexts; specifically, whether a person defines success in terms of self-improvement and task mastery versus normative performance and ability demonstration produces systematically different motivational signatures that persist across time and context.

A mastery goal is an achievement goal in which success is defined by self-improvement, task mastery, and the development of competence relative to prior performance or an absolute task standard; the fundamental purpose is to develop ability rather than to demonstrate it.

A performance goal is an achievement goal in which success is defined by normative superiority — by demonstrating greater ability than others or by avoiding demonstrations of inferior ability; the fundamental purpose is to establish a favorable judgment of one's competence in the eyes of relevant evaluators.

Mastery-approach goal adoption is consistently associated with: intrinsic task motivation, information-seeking behavior (seeking additional explanations, asking questions), adaptive help-seeking, deep processing strategies, positive academic emotions (interest, enjoyment), persistence after failure, reduced test anxiety, and the development of transferable understanding rather than surface performance.

Performance-avoidance goals establish a motivational architecture in which the actor is chronically oriented toward *not failing* rather than toward *succeeding* — a regulatory mode that systematically underinvests in learning, distorts information processing toward threat evaluation, and produces what Covington termed the "self-worth protection" strategy cluster: self-handicapping, procrastination, low persistence, and strategic disengagement.

The mechanism by which performance goals produce the helpless response pattern: (1) Failure encountered → (2) Interpreted against differentiated conception of ability → (3) High effort + failure = evidence of low capacity → (4) Effort withdrawal as self-protective response to protect ability attribution → (5) Performance decrements and disengagement.

Performance-avoidance goal adoption → Competence evaluation construed as threat → Activation of threat appraisal processing (increased self-monitoring, intrusive cognition, anxiety) → Working memory competed for by threat-processing content → Reduced cognitive resources for task performance → Objective performance decrements.

Classroom practices that structure recognition around normative comparison, organize groups by ability, and evaluate on the basis of social ranking collectively instantiate a performance goal structure that, over time, shifts students' adopted goal orientations toward performance goals — even for students who entered the environment with strongly mastery-oriented dispositions.

ordered.text: **Dispositionally adopted** — reflecting stable individual differences in the tendency to approach achievement contexts with mastery versus performance purposes (measured by instruments like the Achievement Goals Questionnaire, AGQ)
**Situationally induced** — activated by features of the immediate context (evaluative instructions, competitive framing, feedback emphasis)
**Socially constructed** — shaped by parents' goal structures and implicit theories, peers' normative behaviors, and teachers' motivational orientations

**Antecedents** (upstream): Implicit theories of intelligence, past achievement history, perceived competence, need for achievement, autonomy support, and attachment security — these construct the motivational terrain
**Achievement Goals** (the level AGT directly addresses): The competence standard and valence structure that organize behavior in achievement contexts
**Consequences** (downstream): Cognitive engagement, affect, attributional reasoning, behavioral persistence or withdrawal, and long-term skill development trajectories

Q: What is the central claim of Achievement Goal Theory? A: That the *purpose* pursued in achievement contexts — specifically whether success is defined by mastery/development versus normative demonstration of ability — determines the cognitive, affective, and behavioral patterns that follow.

Q: What are the two original poles of the dichotomous achievement goal model? A: Mastery goals (success defined by learning, improvement, task mastery) versus performance goals (success defined by normative superiority or avoiding normative inferiority).

Q: Who are the three foundational contributors to AGT and what perspective did each bring? A: Nicholls (developmental — ability conceptions), Dweck (social-cognitive — response patterns and implicit theories), Ames (educational ecology — classroom goal structures).

Q: What is Nicholls' differentiated conception of ability and why does it matter for AGT? A: The belief that ability is a stable capacity distinct from effort, such that high ability means achieving as much as others with *less effort*. It matters because it creates the structural basis for performance goal activation and the threat that failure poses to self-worth.

Q: What two dimensions define the 2×2 achievement goal framework? A: (1) Definition dimension: mastery vs. performance (the competence standard used); (2) Valence dimension: approach vs. avoidance (whether positive or negative possibilities regulate behavior).

Q: Describe the four cells of the 2×2 framework and their associated empirical profiles. A: MAP (pursuing mastery: adaptive), MAV (avoiding mastery failure: mixed), PAP (pursuing normative superiority: mixed — performance benefits but motivational costs), PAV (avoiding normative inferiority: most adverse — anxiety, shallow processing, poor outcomes).

Q: What is the Helpless Response Pattern and what goal orientation predicts it? A: Withdrawal of effort, maladaptive ability attributions, and performance deterioration in response to difficulty; predicted by performance goal orientation because failure implicates low ability when using the differentiated conception.

Q: What is the relationship between implicit theories of intelligence and achievement goal adoption? A: Entity theory (intelligence is fixed) predicts performance goal adoption; incremental theory (intelligence is malleable) predicts mastery goal adoption.

Q: Explain the mechanism by which performance-avoidance goals produce test anxiety costs. A: PAV goals → evaluative cues construed as threats → threat appraisal processing activates → working memory competed for by intrusive threat-relevant cognition → reduced cognitive resources for task performance.

Q: What is the TARGET framework and what role does it play in AGT? A: Ames' taxonomy of classroom design dimensions (Task, Authority, Recognition, Grouping, Evaluation, Time) that collectively constitute the classroom goal structure — specifying the environmental instantiation of mastery vs. performance goal contexts.

Q: Why does high effort under failure become threatening under performance goals but not under mastery goals? A: Under performance goals, the differentiated conception of ability is activated; ability is construed as capacity distinct from effort, so high effort + poor outcome = evidence of low capacity. Under mastery goals, effort is unconditionally valued as the path to development.

Q: What is the practical implication of AGT for feedback design? A: Feedback should emphasize process, effort-as-strategy, and progress toward mastery criteria rather than ability attributions or normative ranking — because praise for intelligence activates the differentiated conception of ability and creates vulnerability.

Q: Why is the performance-approach goal's empirical profile controversial? A: PAP goals predict higher grades and competitive achievement (through approach motivation) but do not predict deep processing, intrinsic motivation, or well-being — suggesting performance benefits are real but narrow, and may be bought at the cost of long-term motivational foundations.

Q: What is meant by "multiple goal adoption" and what does it suggest about the dichotomous model? A: The contemporaneous pursuit of both mastery-approach and performance-approach goals; its frequent adaptive occurrence in competitive academic and sport contexts shows that the early dichotomous model's implied mutual exclusivity was incorrect.

Q: How does AGT relate to Self-Determination Theory? A: Both analyze motivation qualitatively. Mastery goals overlap with SDT's intrinsic/identified motivation; performance-avoidance goals overlap with introjected regulation. AGT organizes around competence standards; SDT organizes around autonomy/control locus.

Q: What is the ecological implication of AGT for educational systems design? A: Goal orientation is not purely dispositional — it is systematically shaped by classroom goal structures. Competitive grading, normative ranking, and ability grouping instantiate performance goal structures that shift modal student goal orientation. Redesigning these structures (per TARGET) is a more powerful intervention than individual mindset coaching alone.

**[[A-focused-analysis-of-mastery-vs.-performance-goal-orientations-and-the-2×2-mode]]** — A dedicated focused analysis examining the empirical controversies surrounding PAP goals, the MAV cell's distinctive profile, and the meta-analytic record in detail.

**[[Growth-Mindset-Theory]]** — Dweck's popular-audience synthesis of incremental theory research; examining both its legitimate empirical foundations and the oversimplifications in its popular reception.

**[[Self-Determination-Theory-—-Foundational-Report]]** — Full foundational treatment of SDT's account of autonomy, competence, and relatedness needs — the upstream framework most richly integrated with AGT.
**[[Feedback-Design-for-Autonomy-and-Mastery]]** — Technical treatment of how AGT and SDT principles are applied in the design of informational, autonomy-supportive feedback systems.

**[[Expectancy-Value-Theory]]** — Eccles and Wigfield's complementary framework that adds subjective task value (intrinsic, utility, attainment value, cost) to the motivational analysis; provides dimensions AGT leaves underspecified.

**[[Self-Regulated-Learning]]** — The broader self-regulation framework within which achievement goals function as a critical motivational component; Zimmerman's cyclical SRL model provides the processual architecture within which AGT constructs operate.

**[[Attribution-Retraining]]** — Intervention literature on modifying causal attributions from ability-based to effort-based explanations for achievement outcomes; the most directly actionable consequence of AGT's mechanistic account.

**[[Metacognition-and-Self-Regulated-Learning]]** — How metacognitive monitoring and control interact with goal orientation; mastery-oriented learners show more adaptive metacognitive calibration and more responsive strategy adjustments.

**Time** — flexible pacing aligned with mastery vs. fixed pacing aligned with schedules and ranking
